subject: physics_2
question_text: Derive an expression for the energy stored in a capacitor. What is the energy stored when the space between the plates is filled with a dielectric (a) With charging battery disconnected? (b) With charging battery connected in the circuit?

verification.note: The 1+2+1+2+2 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Two structural checks are IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the two-book union check (the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only) and the past-paper back-test (the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers). APPEARANCES: the book prints '(2006, 2007-MAY)' beside this question — the only exam-year citation in Chapter 5. The schema's appearance object carries year, q_no and board only, so the MONTH is recorded here and not in the data: the 2007 sitting is the MAY paper. No board is printed, so no board key is set (an absent board means ts_ipe by the schema's own convention). Hand-checked against the book: W = ∫₀^Q (q/C) dq = Q²/2C, so U = Q²/2C = CV²/2 = QV/2; with the battery disconnected Q is fixed, C₀ → KC₀, V = V₀/K and U = Q²/2KC₀ = U₀/K; with the battery connected V is fixed at V₀, Q = KC₀V₀ = KQ₀ and U = KC₀V₀²/2 = KU₀. Every result the book prints is correct. The book's answer text carries two misspellings, not copied: 'the energy stored bocomes' and a scan-blurred 'V≈V₀' where the algebra needs V = V₀; it also uses the older word 'condenser' for capacitor throughout. Transcription: the printed spaces before the two question marks are dropped; nothing else is changed.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The charging work
lines: Take an uncharged capacitor of capacitance C.
To add more charge to a plate that already
carries some, work has to be done against the
potential difference already present.
When the charge on the capacitor is q, that
potential difference is v = q/C.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The charging is done against a potential difference that itself grows.
steps.why: The energy comes out as Q²/2C rather than QV only because the opposing potential difference grows with the charge already delivered — that is the whole physics of the derivation.
common_mistakes: Treating the potential difference as fixed at V throughout the charging.
Starting from a charged capacitor, which leaves no work to add up.

recall.must_convey: That charging is done against the potential difference already on the plates, v = q/C.
accept: work is done against the existing potential
small v equals q by C
reject: d W is v d q

steps.memory_tip: The opposing potential difference grows as the charge grows, so later charge needs more work.

steps.label: The energy integral
lines: The small work done in adding a further
charge dq is dW = v dq. Adding all such
bits of work from q = 0 to q = Q:

lines.text: W = ∫ v dq = ∫ (q/C) dq,  q from 0 to Q

steps.margin_note: Two marks. Write dW = v dq, put v = q/C, integrate between 0 and Q.
steps.why: The integral is what turns a growing potential difference into a single number; the factor of two comes straight out of integrating q, not from any separate rule.
common_mistakes: Writing W = QV by taking v outside the integral.
Losing the limits, so the constant of integration is never removed.

recall.must_convey: That dW = v dq is integrated with v = q/C from 0 to Q, giving W = Q²/2C.
accept: d W is v d q
integrate q by C from zero to Q
W is Q squared by 2 C
reject: work is done against the existing potential

steps.memory_tip: Integrating q gives q²/2 — that is where the half in the energy comes from.

steps.label: The three forms
lines: This work is stored in the capacitor as
electric potential energy U. Using Q = CV,
the same energy can be written in three ways:
Which form is useful depends on whether the
charge or the potential difference is held
fixed, and that is the difference between the
two cases below.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. All three forms, and note that the fixed quantity picks the form.
steps.why: The two dielectric cases are only different because one holds Q fixed and the other holds V fixed, so choosing the matching form is what parts (a) and (b) test.
common_mistakes: Dropping the factor of two and writing CV² or Q²/C.
Giving only one form, then being unable to handle case (a).

recall.must_convey: That U = Q²/2C = CV²/2 = QV/2, and that the form to use depends on which quantity is held fixed.
accept: U is Q squared by 2 C
U is half C V squared
reject: integrate q by C from zero to Q

steps.memory_tip: Q fixed, use Q²/2C. V fixed, use CV²/2. Match the form to the quantity that is constant.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: One circuit for both cases: switch open is (a), battery disconnected; switch closed is (b), battery connected.
steps.why: Drawing one circuit with a switch makes the only difference between the two cases visible — whether the battery is still in the loop when the slab goes in.
common_mistakes: Drawing the slab outside the plates instead of between them.

recall.must_convey: That a capacitor with a dielectric slab between its plates is drawn in a loop with a battery and a switch.
accept: capacitor with a slab between the plates
battery and switch in the loop
switch open or closed for the two cases
reject: U is Q squared by 2 C

steps.memory_tip: Switch open: the charge cannot change. Switch closed: the voltage cannot change.

steps.label: Battery disconnected
lines: (a) With the charging battery disconnected.
Let a capacitor of capacitance C₀ be charged
to a potential difference V₀. Its charge is
Q = C₀V₀ and its stored energy is
The battery is now removed and a slab of
dielectric constant K is placed between the
plates. With no battery in the circuit the
charge Q on the plates cannot change. The
capacitance becomes C = KC₀, so

lines.text: Q fixed: V = V₀/K and U = U₀/K

lines: Both the potential difference and the
energy fall to 1/K of their first values.
steps.margin_note: Two marks. State that Q cannot change, then use the Q²/2C form.
steps.why: With the plates isolated there is no path for charge to leave, so Q is the constant; the energy falls because the field pulls the slab in and does work on it.
common_mistakes: Holding V constant instead of Q, which reverses the answer.
Using CV²/2 with the old V₀, which misses the drop in V.

recall.must_convey: That with the battery disconnected Q stays fixed, so V falls to V₀/K and U falls to U₀/K.
accept: V becomes V nought by K
energy falls to U nought by K
reject: battery keeps the voltage the same

steps.memory_tip: No battery, no path for charge: Q stays the same, so V and U both divide by K.

steps.label: Battery connected
lines: (b) With the charging battery still connected.
The battery holds the potential difference at
V₀, so here it is V that cannot change. The
starting energy is
The same slab makes the capacitance C = KC₀,
and the charge rises to

lines.text: V fixed: Q = KQ₀ and U = KU₀

lines: The charge and the stored energy both rise to K
times their first values, and the extra energy
is supplied by the battery.
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. State that V cannot change, use CV²/2, and name the battery as the source of the extra energy.
steps.why: The battery is still in the loop, so it supplies more charge to hold V at V₀ — the extra energy has to come from somewhere, and saying so is what separates a full answer from a formula.
common_mistakes: Giving U₀/K again by copying case (a).
Not saying where the extra energy comes from.

recall.must_convey: That with the battery connected V stays at V₀, so Q rises to KQ₀ and U rises to KU₀, the extra energy coming from the battery.
accept: battery keeps the voltage the same

steps.memory_tip: Battery in the loop fixes V, so C up by K makes Q and U rise by K too.

insider_note: Half the paper's marks for this question are in the two dielectric cases, so an answer that derives U and stops there scores about four — and the single line the examiner checks first is which of Q and V is held constant in each case.
